ai.definition: Consciousness uploading (CU) is a neurotechnology that involves the digitization and replication of an individual's brain patterns into a virtual environment or artificial body. This process aims to preserve or transfer consciousness beyond physical death.
ai.howItWorks: The neural activity of a person's brain is mapped in detail, capturing the intricate patterns of neurons and synapses. These patterns are then encoded into a digital format that can be stored or transferred. The resulting digital representation can either exist as a virtual entity within a computer-generated environment or inhabit an artificial body designed to support consciousness.
ai.problemSolved: CU addresses the existential concern of human existence beyond physical death, offering a means for preserving individuality and identity in alternative forms. It also opens possibilities for creating new life forms with enhanced cognitive abilities.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves advanced neuroimaging techniques to map brain activity, followed by complex computational algorithms to encode this data into digital form. The creation of an artificial body or virtual environment requires sophisticated robotics and virtual reality technologies.
ai.buildProcess: First, the subject undergoes a series of invasive and non-invasive neuroimaging procedures to capture their brain's neural architecture. This data is then processed using AI algorithms to create a detailed model. Finally, this model is transferred into a digital space or artificial body.
ai.costDrivers: High initial costs due to cutting-edge technology requirements, including advanced imaging equipment, computational power, and specialized software. Long-term costs include maintenance of the digital infrastructure and potential energy consumption.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The field is currently in early-stage research with significant scientific and technical challenges remaining before practical applications can be realized.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations governing consciousness uploading. However, ethical considerations related to consent, privacy, and the nature of identity will likely drive future regulatory frameworks.
ai.risks: Technological risks include errors in data mapping and encoding, potential loss or corruption of uploaded consciousness. Ethical concerns revolve around issues of consent, identity theft, and the moral implications of creating digital entities from human brains.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to current lack of practical applications and regulatory frameworks. Potential for significant economic impact if successful but high development costs and ethical barriers pose challenges.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future advancements may include improvements in neuroimaging techniques, more efficient data encoding algorithms, and the creation of more realistic artificial bodies or virtual environments.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Digital infrastructure requires substantial power for long-term storage and operation.

glossary.def: The process of transferring a human's consciousness into a digital environment or artificial body.
The specific electrical and chemical signals that represent thought processes within the brain.
A computer-generated simulation of a three-dimensional environment that can be interacted with in a seemingly real or physical way.
A robotic or virtual embodiment designed to support and house an uploaded consciousness.

subsystems.name: Tissue preservation and sectioning
subsystems.role: keeps the brain's wiring intact and cuts it into slices thin enough to image.

subsystems.name: Volume imaging
subsystems.role: records every neuron, axon and synapse in three dimensions.

subsystems.name: Connectome reconstruction
subsystems.role: turns millions of images into a traced wiring diagram.
parts: machine-learning segmentation of neurons and synapses

subsystems.name: Cell-type and molecular mapping
subsystems.role: adds what a wiring diagram alone cannot show — which cells are which and how they signal.

subsystems.name: Emulation software
subsystems.role: runs a mathematical model of every neuron and synapse in simulated time.

subsystems.name: Compute substrate
subsystems.role: supplies the enormous, highly parallel processing the emulation needs.

subsystems.name: Embodiment and interface
subsystems.role: gives the emulation senses and actions, or a virtual world to inhabit.

buildSteps.title: Preserve the brain
buildSteps.detail: The tissue is fixed chemically, or in theory vitrified, so that membranes, proteins and synaptic contacts stay in place.

buildSteps.title: Slice and image it
buildSteps.detail: The block is shaved into slices a few tens of nanometres thick and imaged by electron microscope at a resolution of a few nanometres — enough to see a synapse.

buildSteps.title: Reconstruct the wiring
buildSteps.detail: Software stitches the images, traces every axon and dendrite and marks each synapse, producing a graph of roughly 86 billion nodes and 100 trillion connections for a human brain.

buildSteps.title: Annotate cell types and chemistry
buildSteps.detail: Each neuron must be labelled by type, transmitter released and receptor composition — information that imaging alone does not supply and that would come from paired molecular atlases.

buildSteps.title: Capture dynamic state
buildSteps.detail: A static map misses the moment-to-moment voltages and short-term strengths that make a brain a brain; the state would have to be inferred, or read out from a living brain, which no method can currently do at full scale.

buildSteps.title: Build the emulation
buildSteps.detail: Every neuron and synapse becomes a model, connected exactly as mapped, and the whole network is stepped forward in time on a large computer.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate against the real brain
buildSteps.detail: The model's activity patterns are compared with recordings from the living brain it came from, and its parameters adjusted until the two match.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: The emulation is wired to sensors and effectors or to a simulated world, so it receives input and produces output the way a brain does.

buildSteps.title: Test for consciousness
buildSteps.detail: This step is unsolved: no accepted method exists to determine whether a faithful emulation experiences anything, rather than merely behaving as if it does.

prerequisites.why: complete maps exist only for animals with hundreds to hundreds of thousands of neurons; a human brain is about a million times larger in volume and would need petabytes of imagery.

prerequisites.tech: Non-destructive readout of living neural state
prerequisites.why: fixing tissue kills it, so the dynamic state at the moment of scanning cannot be recovered from a dead brain.

prerequisites.tech: Complete models of how neurons compute
prerequisites.why: synaptic strengths, receptor types and dendritic processing are only partly characterised, and simulation accuracy is limited by that uncertainty.
the fastest supercomputers can simulate simplified networks, but running 86 billion detailed neurons with 100 trillion plastic synapses in real time is far beyond them.
without it there is no way to verify that an emulation is a person rather than a convincing simulation of one.

pathway.milestone: complete wiring diagrams of tiny nervous systems — 302 neurons in a nematode, and in 2024 the roughly 140,000 neurons of an adult fruit fly
pathway.unlocks: proof that automated reconstruction works, at least for small brains.

pathway.milestone: partial maps of mammalian cortex and paired maps of structure plus cell type and activity
pathway.unlocks: rules for how wiring relates to function, and better automated tracing.

pathway.milestone: emulation of a small mammal brain at reduced speed, behaving recognisably
pathway.unlocks: evidence that structure-based simulation can reproduce real behaviour.

pathway.milestone: human-scale emulation, if the imaging, compute and verification problems are ever solved together
pathway.unlocks: a claimed digital continuation of a mind — and hard questions about consent, identity and whether the copy is anyone at all.
